newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greece, Portugal, Luxembourg ask for telecoms delays.
newsitem.headline: Greece, Portugal, Luxembourg ask for telecoms delays.

text.p: Greece, Portugal and Luxembourg have formally asked the European Commission for permission to delay fully liberalising their telecommunications markets, the Commission said.
Greece said it wanted to wait until 2003 and Luxembourg and Portugal until 2000, according to notices published in the Official Journal.
They all said that their national phone companies needed more time to adjust before facing full competition.
The European Commission adopted a directive this year, 96/19/EC, requiring EU states to abolish state monopolies over voice telephone by January 1, 1998.
It also ordered them to allow operators of "alternative" telecoms networks to compete with the traditional monopolies to carry some services by July 1, 1996.
But it said Luxembourg could request a delay of up to two years and Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain of up to five years on the grounds that they had small or less developed networks.

Ireland has already asked to wait until 2000 to open up voice telephone services and networks and until July 1, 1999 to allow alternative networks to compete. Spain has so far not made an official request.

Greece told the Commission that it needed the full five-year transition periods for both voice telephone and alternative networks, according to OJ C257. It said full competition in 1998 would prejudice the investment programme that national company OTE had launched for digitalisation and general modernisation.

"The constraints on Greece's financial resources, the high cost and the size of OTE's modernisation programme, aggravated by the considerable expense of delivering telecommunications services throughout the Greek territory...necessitate a gradual pace of modernization," it argued.
Early liberalisation of alternative infrastructure would deprive OTE of significant revenue needed to modernise, it said.
Portugal asked to wait until January 1, 2000 to liberalise voice telephone and until July 1, 1999, for alternative infrastructure, a notice in OJ C260 said.

It said Portugal Telecom earned about six percent of its revenues from providing leased circuits. Immediate lifting of restrictions on alternative networks could lead to a loss of 24 billion Escudos over five years, it said.
That would affect the company's ability to finance "universal service" -- the provision of affordable basic phone service to all citizens, it said.
Portugal said the company needed more time to restructure and the government needed to complete studies on "rebalancing" tariffs to bring them in line with costs.
Luxembourg said it wanted to take advantage of its full two-year transition periods -- until January 1, 2000 for voice telephone and July 1, 1998 for alternative infrastructure.
It did not want to liberalise its markets before a suitable regulatory framework was in place and national operator EPT had restructured, a notice in OJ C257 said.

International calls accounted for 71 percent of EPT's overall turnover in 1995. Premature opening up of the market would allow telecoms companies from other countries to divert that business, posing a serious threat to the company's future development in a competitive market, it argued.
The Commission said it was seeking comments from EU governments and other interested parties before deciding on the three requests.
